groups.title: Message Queue Fundamentals
groups.question: Explain why an API would send work to a queue instead of doing it during the request, and how that is set up.

followUps.Why Queues — Decoupling, Retries & Backp: Sending a welcome email makes sign-up slow. How does a queue fix that?
followUps.BullMQ — Queues, Jobs & Workers: What are the producer, the queue and the worker in BullMQ, and why run workers separately?

evidence.text: The API puts a job on a queue and responds right away instead of waiting for the slow task.
A separate worker does the slow work in the background.
If the email service is slow or down, jobs wait and retry instead of failing the sign-up.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (queue, async, background job) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says the queue makes the email itself send faster.

evidence.text: The producer, such as the API, adds jobs.
The queue holds waiting jobs, in Redis for BullMQ.
Workers process jobs in their own processes, so they can be scaled or restarted without touching the API.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (BullMQ, producer, worker) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says the worker has to run inside the API process.

groups.title: Reliability Patterns
groups.question: Explain how you make background jobs survive failures without doing harm.

followUps.Retries, Exponential Backoff & Dead-Lett: Why wait longer between each retry, and where does a job go when it keeps failing?
followUps.Job Idempotency: A job that charges a card runs twice after a retry. How do you make that safe?

evidence.text: Each retry waits longer than the last (exponential backoff, often with jitter) so a struggling service isn't hammered.
After the last retry the job goes to a failed or dead-letter queue, where it can be inspected and replayed.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (retries, backoff, DLQ) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says jobs should be retried immediately and forever until they succeed.

evidence.text: A retried job can repeat a side effect, such as charging the card twice.
An idempotency key or unique job id lets the payment provider or your database recognise a repeat.
Before acting, the job checks whether the work was already done and skips it if so.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (idempotent, idempotency key) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says the fix is to turn retries off.

groups.title: Webhooks
groups.question: Explain how webhooks work, both when your API sends them and when it receives them.

followUps.Sending Webhooks — Delivery Guarantees &: The receiver is down when you send a webhook. What should your system do?
followUps.Receiving Webhooks — HMAC Signature Veri: How does an HMAC signature prove a webhook really came from the sender?

evidence.text: Deliveries are queued and retried with backoff when the receiver is down.
Each attempt and its result is stored, so failures can be seen and replayed.
After repeated failures the delivery is marked failed and someone is alerted, instead of silently dropping it.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (webhook, retry) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says the receiver will fetch missed events on its own.

evidence.text: The sender and the receiver share a secret.
The sender computes an HMAC of the raw body with that secret and sends it in a header.
The receiver recomputes it from the raw body and compares; a match proves who sent it and that it wasn't changed.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (HMAC, signature) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says the HMAC encrypts the payload so nobody else can read it.

groups.title: Scheduled & Delayed Jobs
groups.question: Explain how you would run jobs later or on a schedule, and keep an eye on your queues.

followUps.Delayed Jobs & Cron Scheduling with Bull: Why is setInterval a bad scheduler when your API runs as several processes?
followUps.Monitoring Queues — BullBoard: Which queue numbers would warn you that workers are falling behind?

evidence.text: Every process runs its own setInterval, so with N instances the job runs N times.
Timers live in memory and are lost when a process restarts or redeploys.
A queue or scheduler with a single owner, like BullMQ repeatable jobs or a lock, runs it exactly once.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (setInterval, cron, repeatable jobs) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says setInterval is only a problem because it isn't exact to the millisecond.

evidence.text: A growing number of waiting jobs means workers can't keep up.
Rising failed jobs or retries mean jobs are breaking.
The age of the oldest waiting job, or processing time, shows the delay users actually feel.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (BullBoard, queue metrics) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says the completed count alone shows the queue is healthy.
